content: Gastrointestinal bleeding, also referred to as gastrointestinal hemorrhage, is defined as the loss of blood from any part of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, which extends from the mouth to the anus. Depending on the site of origin, it is classified into upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) and lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB). Upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) originates from a site proximal to the ligament of Treitz, while lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB) arises from a site distal to the ligament of Treitz. The most common causes of UGIB include peptic ulcer disease and esophageal varices, whereas diverticulosis is the leading cause of LGIB. Patients with gastrointestinal bleeding may present with overt bleeding, which can occur rapidly or slowly. Clinical manifestations include hematemesis, which is the vomiting of fresh red blood or altered blood that appears as coffee ground vomitus. Other presentations include melena, characterized by the passage of black, tarry stools, and hematochezia, which is the passage of bright red blood per rectum. Hematochezia is typically associated with lower GI bleeding but can also result from massive upper GI bleeding. Risk factors for the development of gastrointestinal bleeding include advanced age, a prior history of GI bleeding, chronic constipation, hematologic disorders, and the use of medications such as anticoagulants and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It is crucial to differentiate between lower GI bleeding and brisk upper GI bleeding, as they may present with similar symptoms. Patients with severe bleeding or hemodynamic instability require hospitalization and urgent diagnostic evaluation. The management of gastrointestinal bleeding depends on the underlying cause and the severity of the bleeding. The types of bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract include the following: Hematemesis: Vomiting of fresh red blood. Coffee ground emesis: Vomiting of altered, black-colored blood. Melena: Passage of black, tarry stools. Hematochezia: Passage of bright red blood per rectum, usually due to lower GI bleeding but occasionally caused by massive upper GI bleeding. Rebleeding: Defined as the recurrence of fresh hematemesis and/or melena, accompanied by signs of shock such as a pulse rate exceeding 100 beats per minute, systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg, a central venous pressure (CVP) drop greater than 5 mmHg, or a hemoglobin concentration decrease of more than 20 g/L within 24 hours. Rebleeding must always be confirmed through endoscopy.
